output.best_reason: Version A is the most controlled. Girard's voice is clipped and proud, with a suspicious edge ("I was not waiting for anything," "I had a figure to think about"). The timings come out through short, pointed questions, so the reader senses what Girard is holding back without being told. Version B is close behind, with good beats like "To ask him for my money" and "You are sure of the time?". Version C has the sharpest lines and the most tension, but it opens with a drafting note that is not part of the fiction, which breaks the reading experience. Version E is warm and humane, but its colloquial phrasing ("It's a terrible thing," "can't") loosens the period feel, and Girard confesses too freely to build much pressure. Version D delivers the facts in long, self-explanatory monologues, so they read as recited, and it has the least tension of the five.
